standard.title: Combinations for Two Events
standard.description: determine all possible combinations for 2 events, using two-way tables, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams, and use these to determine probabilities of specific outcomes in practical situations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can list sample spaces and assign probabilities for single-stage events (from AC9M7P01). Students understand complementary events (from AC9M8P01).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students represent all combinations for two events using two-way tables, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams, and calculate probabilities of compound events.

nodes.label: Representing two-event combinations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students represent all possible combinations for two events using two-way tables, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams.
nodes.minimum_width: Represent all combinations for two events using one of: two-way table, tree diagram, or Venn diagram.
nodes.typical_width: Represent the same two-event situation using all three methods; identify which representation is most useful for different probability questions.
wider: Explore First Nations Australian children's instructive games with two-event outcomes — e.g. Battendi from the Ngarrindjeri Peoples — represent combinations and discuss fairness.
Investigate mutually exclusive events using Venn diagrams: show that the circles don't overlap and explain what this means.

response_modes.reason: Each representation (table, tree, Venn) makes different probability questions easy or hard. Students need experience with all three to develop judgment about which to use for a given question.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot select an appropriate representation for a given probability question cannot access Node 2 — calculating compound event probabilities requires first constructing a valid representation of the sample space.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations games as a probability context and the systematic comparison of all three representation types offer advancing students both cultural richness and mathematical depth — comparing which representation best answers which question is a genuine reasoning task.
success_criteria: Correctly lists all combinations for a two-event situation.
Represents combinations accurately using at least one method.
Identifies the advantage of each representation for different questions.

nodes.label: Calculating compound event probabilities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students use representations to calculate probabilities of compound events using 'and', 'or' (inclusive and exclusive), and 'at least' language.
nodes.minimum_width: Calculate P(A and B) and P(A or B) from a two-way table or Venn diagram.
nodes.typical_width: Calculate probabilities using all event language types (and, or, at least, not); distinguish inclusive and exclusive or; apply to practical situations.
wider: Investigate the addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) informally — verify using a two-way table.
Apply compound probability to real situations: the probability of a randomly selected student studying both maths and music, or either subject.

response_modes.reason: Compound probability calculation requires careful interpretation of event language before selecting a calculation method. Students who skip the interpretation step frequently calculate the wrong compound event.

success_criteria: Correctly calculates P(A and B) and P(A or B) from a representation.
Distinguishes inclusive and exclusive 'or' in context.
Uses the representation systematically rather than guessing.
